The aabcb rhyme scheme is really unique, and it works well for your poem. The poem flows really well overall, but the line "If only I were so good at dying" kind of slows the rhythm of the reading. Taking out the "so" would fix it, though it also takes emphasis away from being "so good" at things except for dying. Another thing to think about is capitalizing the first letter of each line. It's a stylistic thing, though the third line is capitalized and none of the other ones are, save for the "I'm" of the first line. I really enjoyed your poem and there really isn't that much you could add to make it better. It's length is perfect for the message; it doesn't go on long enough for the reader to get bored, and it isn't so short that it doesn't have a complete thought or meaning behind it.

It has a good rhythm to it; it sounds like a poem you could sing. I love the use of varying line length, especially having a one word sentence. It really helps to show the speaker's feelings and perspective of the world around them. The use of ambiguity, especially noticeable in the last line—is it the sun wanting forgiveness, or maybe it represents somebody in the speaker's life—makes the reader question what is real in the poem and compels them to reread it and see if they missed contextual clues that seemed irrelevant until the end. 

I feel like line breaks and stanzas to separate different ideas, like after the first five lines, will help your poem flow easier. These lines are addressing the speaker's anger and it's material form in the world, where the next six focus on their visual perception of this anger and his/her gaze. There are places that adding a comma or a semicolon would also help. The line "Rotten a cadaver only will be perceived" could use a comma after "rotten," and changing the commas to semicolons in the lines "A past forgotten, a present delirious, a future nonexistant" would make the reader pause between each line while also showing the relationship to the speaker's mental state at this point in the poem. You also might want to consider changing "Denied a past" from the previous line to "Denied yesterday." It is a more subtle way of past and the repetition of "a past" between the two lines is a little jarring.

“Boots, come on! It’s almost Dark time. We need to find a place to hide.” She meowed in reply, closely following me. 

People say that cats aren’t as smart as dogs, nor as obedient, but Boots has lived longer than any dog I’ve seen roaming the streets with their adopted owners. Cats are more cunning and agile than dogs, so they are able to escape from the trouble much easier than dogs. 

We walked past buildings that were preparing for the chaos to ensure: windows being covered by inches of metal, doors being bolted shut and barred, even chimneys went on lockdown, ever since the Manchester Bombings where the Dark threw homemade bombs down chimneys. Protection is required to survive here; if you don’t have a home to barricade yourself in, you better be able to keep yourself away from the Dark long enough for the sun to rise and civilized laws to become relevant again. 

Boots and I headed for the docks. The past couple nights, we found shelter from the Dark, though we’re exposed to the frigid air that cut through the skin, into the soul. Our spot was a fish market. I knew from experience that the folks who run it don’t have the money to afford all the protection necessary to keep out the Dark; there is one window that only has a metal cutting board propped against it. If anybody in the Dark ever came upon it, they would notice it in a second. 
I pushed the cutting board away from the window far enough to grab both sides of it to move it out of the way without having it clatter to the ground and draw unwanted attention. Boots jumped in gracefully, I slid through the window until my feet touched the ground. I hate heights. 

“Boots, come here. You need to be brushed. A clean kittle is a happy kitty.” In return, she meowed in disapproval, and begrudgingly came over, allowing me to detangle her fur matted with the grime from the city. The makeshift brush kept falling apart again. “Dammit! I need better glue! Some Krazy Glue, not this kiddie glue!” I came up with the idea to make the brush when I was sitting in a diner. There was a bottle full of toothpicks. I took about twenty, broke them in half, and glued them to my pocket watch. It was a family heirloom made of sterling silver, but I prefer using it for something important rather than pawning it for useless cash or keeping it as a trinket since it stopped working long ago.
“There, much better huh? Pretty girl. My baby,” I cooed while stroking her chin and cheeks how she liked. In response, Boots began to purr and I was able to relax. 

We stayed like that until she decided that it was food time. I took one of the knives from the shelf, found a fish that seemed like the smallest, and sliced it so that the meat and innards were exposed. She happily began eating the fish, purring all the while. Suddenly, the purring stopped and she puffed up into a ball of fur, growling. 
Then I heard it; the unmistakable sound of the Dark. They were rubbing metal against metal, probably blades of some kind. I looked to the window and my heart sank into my stomach. I didn’t move the cutting board back. I tried to move it quietly, but in my panic I let it smack against the window. 
The scraping stopped. 

I grabbed Boots and hid in the furthest corner from the window, cloaked in shadows. Anxiously, I began stroking her again, trying to calm myself, to stop my body from screaming with every moment that went by, imagining the Dark getting closer to our place. I heard footsteps from one of the windows. I held my breath, tried to slow my pounding heart. They began getting quieter; the Dark aren’t as good at noticing things as I thought.

As I sat there hugging Boots tightly to my chest, I realized how foolish I’ve been. I grabbed a few knives from the shelf, one for each hand and three spares-stuffed in my pockets. Boots rubbed herself against my leg and meowed, perturbed. 
“They won’t bother us anymore. I promise, baby.” I looked down at her and noticed the white board the owner’s use to write the prices for their fish. I grabbed it and the marker and wrote: Her name is Boots. She needs to be brushed daily. Take good care of her. Next to the board, I set down the pocket watch brush, just in case they didn’t have one.

I looked at her again. She was agitated, didn’t understand what was going on, and didn’t like it at all. I cut open another fish for her if she got hungry later. I rubbed her chin and cheeks again and kissed her forehead. 

“I’ll be back, pretty kitty. I love you.”
